newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu angers Moslems over Jerusalem model.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu angers Moslems over Jerusalem model.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu's office apologised on Sunday over a map the Israeli prime minister gave a Greek Orthodox archbishop depicting a Jewish temple at the heart of Jerusalem's Old City in place of Moslem shrines.
The silver relief map showed a rebuilt Jewish shrine atop Jerusalem's Temple Mount, where Islam's Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa mosques now stand.
The gift infuriated Moslems who viewed it as a challenge to their religious rights in Jerusalem. The mosque compound, where a Jewish temple stood 2,000 years ago, is Islam's third holiest shrine.
"It was a mistake. If the event harmed the feelings of the public, we apologise," Netanyahu's spokesman told Reuters.
"We didn't notice that the al-Aqsa mosque was missing on the relief, there certainly was no intention on our part to hurt any population and this happened due to lack of attention."
Israel's Haaretz newspaper reported on Sunday that Netanyahu gave the gift to the Greek Orthodox Archbishop of Israel, Maximus Salum, as a Christmas and New Year's present last month.
"What could I have done, return the gift to the prime minister?" Haaretz quoted the archbishop as saying.
Sheikh Ikrima Sabri, the Palestinian Mufti of Jerusalem, called the right-wing Likud leader's gift "racist".

"This reiterates that the policies of the Likud towards Jerusalem are racist and aggressive because the Likud only believes in replacing the al-Aqsa and other holy Moslem sites with the Jewish temple," Sabri told Reuters.
"Netanyahu has allowed himself to violate the holiness of the Moslem shrines and this is a challenge to Moslem feelings."

Jerusalem is a city holy to Jews, Christians and Moslems. Israel occupied the city's Arab eastern half, including the Old City, in the 1967 Middle East war and later declared the entire city its eternal capital.
Palestinians want Arab East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. Interim Israeli-PLO peace deals leave the city's fate up to "final status" talks due to be completed in 1999.
